column9: stem
column14: option_a
column15: option_b
column16: option_c
column28: explanation
column29: hint

column9: Protists are **eukaryotic**. What does that tell you about their cells?
column14: Their DNA floats loose in the cytoplasm
column15: They are made of many cells
column16: Their cells have a nucleus
column28: Eukaryotic means the cells have a nucleus and other membrane-bound organelles. DNA floating loose in the cytoplasm describes bacteria (prokaryotes), which have no nucleus. Protists can be one-celled or many-celled, and they can be autotrophs or heterotrophs, so those choices are not what eukaryotic means.
column29: What structure do protist cells have that bacteria cells do not?

column9: Mr. Erickson sorts the Kingdom Protista into three main types. What are they?
column14: Producers, consumers, and decomposers
column15: Plant-like, animal-like, and fungus-like
column16: Algae, mosses, and mushrooms
column28: Protists are sorted by which other kingdom they act like: plant-like (algae), animal-like (protozoans), and fungus-like (slime molds and water molds). Mosses and mushrooms belong to other kingdoms, and producers, consumers, and decomposers are ecology roles, not protist types.
column29: Each type is named after another kingdom that the protist resembles.

column9: Animal-like protists are also called ___, a name that means "first animals."
column28: Animal-like protists are protozoans (protozoa means "first animals"). They are one-celled heterotrophs that can move, and they are classified by how they move.
column29: It's the group name for amoebas, paramecia, and the other one-celled heterotrophs that move.

column9: Most protists are unicellular, but some form simple multicellular structures or colonies.
column28: True. Most protists are one-celled. Some, like kelp or Volvox colonies, are many-celled or live in colonies, but they have very little tissue specialization.
column29: Compare an amoeba with a giant kelp.

column9: Animal-like protists are grouped into categories based on what?
column14: Their color
column15: Their shape
column16: How big they grow
column28: Protozoans are classified by their method of movement: pseudopods, cilia, flagella, or no movement at all. Color is how algae (plant-like protists) are grouped.
column29: Think about what pseudopods, cilia, and flagella are all used for.

column9: What does an amoeba use to move?
column14: Pseudopods (false feet)
column15: Cilia (short hairs)
column16: Flagella (whip-like tails)
column28: Amoebas (sarcodines) push out pseudopods, extensions of the cell membrane and cytoplasm whose name means "false foot," and flow forward. Cilia belong to ciliates like paramecium, flagella to flagellates, and spores are how sporozoans reproduce.
column29: Picture an amoeba moving: its shape keeps changing as parts of the cell bulge outward.

column9: Single-celled algae that float near the surface of the water and feed many marine animals are called ___.
column28: Phytoplankton are single-celled, floating algae. They are an important food source for marine animals and make a large share of Earth's oxygen. Zooplankton are the tiny animals and animal-like protists that drift in the water and eat phytoplankton.
column29: These are the plant-like drifters at the bottom of the ocean food chain.

column9: Which group of algae includes kelp?
column14: Red algae
column15: Brown algae
column16: Golden algae
column28: Kelp is a large, many-celled brown alga. Brown algae give food and shelter to marine animals. Red algae live deep in the ocean, golden algae include diatoms, and green algae include Volvox and Spirogyra.
column29: Kelp is a giant seaweed. Which group of algae is made of large, many-celled seaweeds?

column9: Algae are classified mainly by what?
column14: How they move
column15: Which animal they infect
column16: Their color and structure
column28: Algae are grouped by color (red, brown, golden, green) and structure. All algae have chlorophyll, but extra (accessory) pigments give some groups a different color. Movement is how protozoans are grouped.
column29: Think about the names of the algae groups you learned.

column9: What are the two kinds of fungus-like protists?
column14: Slime molds and water molds
column15: Bread molds and mushrooms
column16: Diatoms and dinoflagellates
column28: The fungus-like protists are slime molds and water molds. Bread molds, mushrooms, yeasts, and lichens involve true fungi (Kingdom Fungi), and diatoms and dinoflagellates are plant-like protists.
column29: Cross out any pair that contains a true fungus or an alga.

column9: Red and brown algae contain no chlorophyll, which is why they are not green.
column28: False. All algae contain chlorophyll a, which they need for photosynthesis. In red and brown algae, extra (accessory) pigments cover up the green color.
column29: Can an alga do photosynthesis without chlorophyll?

column9: Match each group of protozoans to its description.
column14: Sarcodines :: Pseudopods (false feet)
column15: Ciliates :: Many short cilia that beat in waves
column16: Flagellates :: One or more long, whip-like flagella
column28: Protozoans are classified by movement: sarcodines (amoebas) use pseudopods, ciliates (paramecium) use cilia, flagellates use flagella, and sporozoans (Plasmodium) do not move on their own.
column29: Two group names hint at the structure they use. The sporozoans are named for how they reproduce, not how they move.

column9: An amoeba flows around a smaller protist, wraps part of its cell around it, and pulls it inside. What is this process called?
column14: Photosynthesis
column15: Conjugation
column16: Binary fission
column28: Phagocytosis means engulfing food. The amoeba wraps part of its cell around its prey, and the food ends up in a food vacuole where it is digested. Photosynthesis makes food from light, conjugation is swapping genetic material, and binary fission is splitting in two.
column29: Phago- means "eating."

column9: Most protists reproduce asexually by splitting into two identical cells. What is this called?
column14: Conjugation
column15: Budding
column16: Pollination
column28: In binary fission, one cell splits into two identical cells. Conjugation is the sexual process where two protists join and exchange genetic material. Budding is how yeast reproduces, and pollination happens in flowering plants.
column29: This is the same way bacteria copy themselves.

column9: All protists are heterotrophs that must eat other organisms.
column28: False. Most protists are heterotrophs, but plant-like protists (algae) are autotrophs with chloroplasts, and some, like Euglena, can be both.
column29: Think about algae. Where do they get their food?

column9: Jada finds a single-celled organism in pond water. It has chloroplasts and makes its own food in the light, but when kept in a dark cupboard it swims with a flagellum and takes in food. Which protist is it most likely?
column14: Amoeba
column15: Paramecium
column16: Euglena
column28: Euglena has chloroplasts, so it makes its own food in the light (autotroph). In the dark it can take in food (heterotroph), and it swims with a flagellum and senses light with an eyespot. Amoebas and paramecia have no chloroplasts, and Plasmodium is a parasite that does not move.
column29: Rule out the protists that can only take in food and can never make their own.

column9: Match each part of a paramecium to its job.
column14: Cilia :: Move the cell and sweep food in
column15: Oral groove :: Opening where food enters the cell
column16: Contractile vacuole :: Squeezes extra water out of the cell
column17: Anal pore :: Where wastes leave the cell
column28: A paramecium's cilia move it and sweep food (usually bacteria) into the oral groove, where a food vacuole forms. The contractile vacuole forces out extra water that leaks in from the pond, and wastes leave through the anal pore.
column29: Follow the food: how it gets swept in, where it enters, and where the leftovers leave.

column9: Which products come from algae? Select all that apply.
column14: Chemicals used to make waxes, plastics, and paints
column15: Algin, used to thicken marshmallows
column16: Carrageenan, used to make ice cream and pudding creamy
column17: Yeast, used to make bread dough rise
column28: Carrageenan (from red algae), algin (from brown algae), and chemicals for waxes, plastics, paints, and lubricants all come from algae. Penicillin comes from the mold Penicillium, and yeast is a fungus, so those come from Kingdom Fungi.
column29: Two of the choices come from a different kingdom.

column9: What is a **food vacuole**?
column14: A membrane-bound sac that contains digestive enzymes
column15: A whip-like tail used for swimming
column16: A short hair that sweeps food into the cell
column17: A green organelle that makes sugar from light
column28: A food vacuole is a membrane-bound sac with digestive enzymes. Protozoans digest captured food inside it, and the digested food is absorbed into the cytoplasm. A whip-like tail is a flagellum, a short hair is a cilium, and a green organelle that makes sugar is a chloroplast.
column29: The name tells you what goes inside it.

column9: Amoebas can live in soil as well as in fresh water and the ocean.
column28: True. Amoebas are found in fresh water (aquatic) and salt water (marine) environments and also in the soil. Some even live inside hosts as parasites.
column29: Amoebas need moisture, but not necessarily a pond.

column9: Which disease is caused by a flagellate?
column14: Malaria
column15: African sleeping sickness
column16: Amoebic dysentery
column28: Flagellates are protozoans that swim with flagella, and some are parasites that cause African sleeping sickness (and Giardia, an intestinal illness). Malaria is caused by a sporozoan, amoebic dysentery by an amoeba (sarcodine), and red tide by a dinoflagellate toxin.
column29: Match each disease to the protist group that causes it, then find the flagellate.

column9: Put the steps of the malaria (Plasmodium) life cycle in order, starting with the first bite.
column14: Plasmodium travels to the mosquito's salivary glands
column15: A mosquito bites a person who has malaria
column16: Plasmodium multiplies in the person's blood cells and releases spores
column18: The mosquito bites a healthy person, and Plasmodium enters the bloodstream
column28: The mosquito picks up Plasmodium from an infected person. It moves from the mosquito's stomach to its salivary glands, the next bite injects it into a new person, and it multiplies inside red blood cells until they burst and release spores that infect more cells.
column29: The parasite has to reach the mosquito's saliva before the next bite can pass it on.

column9: Why is Plasmodium hard for the human immune system to fight?
column14: It is covered by a hard, glass-like shell
column15: It swims too fast for white blood cells
column16: It makes its own food by photosynthesis
column17: It hides inside red blood cells
column28: Plasmodium enters red blood cells and makes spores there, where it is hidden from the immune system. When the cells burst, the spores infect more red blood cells. It has no shell, can't move at all, and does not photosynthesize.
column29: Think about where Plasmodium spends its time in the body.

column9: On a hike, Marcus finds a glistening yellow, jelly-like mass spreading slowly over a rotting log. A week later it has turned into small, stationary stalks. What is it most likely?
column14: A slime mold
column15: A water mold
column16: A brown alga
column28: Slime molds grow on damp soil, rotting logs, and decaying leaves as glistening white, red, or yellow masses. They spend part of their life in a moving, amoeba-like feeding form and part in a stationary reproductive stage. Water molds are mostly aquatic, algae need water and light, and sporozoans live inside hosts.
column29: Look at where he found it and how it changed over the week.

column9: Priya notices white, fuzzy growth on a sick goldfish in her aquarium. Which protist most likely causes this?
column14: A slime mold
column15: A diatom
column16: A water mold
column28: Water molds are fungus-like protists made of branching filaments. Most live in water, some are parasites, and they are sometimes seen as white fuzz on diseased aquarium fish. Slime molds live on land, diatoms are algae, and amoebas don't form fuzz.
column29: First find the choices that are fungus-like protists. Then ask which of those is made of branching filaments.

column9: Which statements describe sporozoans like Plasmodium? Select all that apply.
column14: They make their own food with chloroplasts
column15: They reproduce by spores
column16: Some, like Plasmodium, live in the host's blood
column18: They absorb food from their host's cells
column28: Sporozoans are always parasitic, reproduce by spores, and absorb food from the host's cells. Some, like Plasmodium, live in the host's blood (others, like Cryptosporidium, live in the intestine). They have no chloroplasts (they are heterotrophs) and no pseudopods (that's amoebas).
column29: Plasmodium causes malaria. Think about where it lives in a person and what it can't do on its own.

column9: Which of these are plant-like protists? Select all that apply.
column14: Euglena
column15: Kelp
column16: Paramecium
column28: Plant-like protists have chloroplasts and make their own food: kelp (brown algae), diatoms (golden algae), dinoflagellates (fire algae), and Euglena. Paramecium is an animal-like ciliate, and slime mold is a fungus-like protist.
column29: Plant-like protists have chloroplasts. Which of these can make their own food?

column9: Protists supply about half of the world's oxygen. How?
column14: Protozoans release oxygen when they digest food
column15: Floating algae release oxygen during photosynthesis
column16: Slime molds release oxygen as they break down logs
column17: Plasmodium releases oxygen from red blood cells
column28: Single-celled algae have chloroplasts. Like plants, they do photosynthesis and release oxygen, and there are so many of them in the oceans that they make about half of Earth's oxygen. Digesting and decomposing use oxygen rather than make it.
column29: Which process makes oxygen? Which protists can do it?

column9: Fishermen notice the ocean turning reddish, and dead fish wash up on shore. Shellfish from the area are declared unsafe to eat. What is the most likely cause?
column14: A water mold spreading through the fish population
column15: A population explosion of toxic dinoflagellates
column16: A huge kelp bloom blocking out the sunlight
column17: Amoebas from sewage infecting the fish and shellfish
column28: Some species of dinoflagellates (fire algae) make toxins. When their population explodes in one area, the water can turn red (a red tide), killing marine life and contaminating the fish and shellfish we eat. Kelp doesn't turn water red or make toxins.
column29: Which plant-like protist has a red pigment and can make a poison?

column9: When these golden algae die, their hard, box-like shells don't decompose. The shells pile up on the ocean floor and are mined for toothpaste grit, scouring powder, and water filters. What are these protists?
column14: Dinoflagellates
column15: Euglena
column16: Diatoms
column28: Diatoms are golden algae with hard, box-like shells. Their shells collect in layers called diatomaceous earth, which is used as grit, in filters and insulation, and in reflective highway paint. Dinoflagellates are fire algae, Euglena has no shell, and kelp is a brown alga.
column29: The deposits these shells form are named after the protist.

column9: A paramecium has two nuclei that do different jobs. The one that controls everyday cell activities is called the ___.
column28: A paramecium has a large macronucleus that runs everyday cell activities and a small micronucleus that controls reproduction.
column29: Its name compares its size with the other nucleus.

column9: In conjugation, two paramecia join and exchange genetic information.
column28: True. Conjugation is a form of sexual reproduction. Two protists attach and swap genetic material, which creates new combinations of traits. Most of the time protozoans reproduce asexually by binary fission instead.
column29: Conjugation is the sexual way some protozoans reproduce. What gets shared?

column9: After drinking untreated water on a trip to the tropics, Mateo gets bloody diarrhea and stomach cramps. Doctors find a one-celled parasite that moves with pseudopods in his intestines. What disease does he have?
column14: Malaria
column15: African sleeping sickness
column16: Red tide poisoning
column28: A one-celled parasite that moves with pseudopods is an amoeba. Amoebic dysentery is an intestinal infection caused by the amoeba Entamoeba histolytica, picked up from contaminated food or water. It causes bloody diarrhea and cramps. Malaria comes from a mosquito bite, sleeping sickness from a tsetse fly bite, and red tide poisoning from eating contaminated shellfish.
column29: Which protozoan group moves with pseudopods? Which disease on the list does that group cause?

column9: An amoeba lives in a person's intestine, feeds there, and damages the intestinal wall. What type of symbiotic relationship is this?
column14: Parasitism
column15: Mutualism
column16: Commensalism
column28: In parasitism, one organism (the parasite) benefits while the host is harmed. The amoeba gets food and a home, and the person is harmed. In mutualism both benefit, in commensalism one benefits and the other is unaffected, and competition is not a living-together relationship.
column29: Who benefits, and who is harmed?

column9: In 1993, about 403,000 people in Milwaukee got diarrhea and stomach cramps from the protozoan *Cryptosporidium*. Cases showed up all over the city within days. How did most of them get infected?
column14: From mosquito bites
column15: By drinking contaminated tap water
column16: From eating undercooked pork
column17: From coughs and sneezes of sick people
column28: Heavy spring runoff carried Cryptosporidium oocysts into Lake Michigan (the exact source was never proven; farm runoff and sewage were both suspected), and they got through the treatment plant into the city's drinking water. Tap water reaches homes all over a city at once, which fits cases appearing everywhere within days. Officials now order people to boil water when treatment fails. Mosquitoes spread malaria, not Cryptosporidium, and Cryptosporidium is not spread by coughs or by pork.
column29: What did all 403,000 people have in common in their daily routine?

column9: Ava's lab group finds an organism in pond water. It has a nucleus, it is made of one cell, its surface is covered with hundreds of tiny hairs that beat to move it, and it eats bacteria. Where does it belong?
column14: Kingdom Protista, with the flagellates
column15: Kingdom Animalia, because it moves and eats
column16: With the bacteria, because it is one cell
column28: It has a nucleus (eukaryotic) and is one cell, so it is not a bacterium (no nucleus) and not an animal (animals are multicellular). The tiny beating hairs are cilia, and moving with cilia puts it with the ciliates, like the paramecium.
column29: Check two things first: does it have a nucleus, and is it one cell or many?

column9: Under the microscope, organism A flows slowly and keeps changing shape, organism B glides in smooth, straight lines, and organism C moves in a jerky zig-zag. Which structures are they most likely using?
column14: A: pseudopods, B: cilia, C: a flagellum
column15: A: cilia, B: pseudopods, C: a flagellum
column16: A: a flagellum, B: cilia, C: pseudopods
column17: A: pseudopods, B: a flagellum, C: cilia
column28: Organisms with pseudopods appear to flow. Many cilia beating together give smooth, straight movement. A whipping flagellum gives a zig-zag path (like Euglena).
column29: Many tiny hairs beating together give a smooth ride. A single whip gives a jerky one.

column9: A village wants to cut down on malaria. Which plan attacks the Plasmodium life cycle most directly?
column14: Boil all drinking water for five minutes before use
column15: Wash all salad greens well before eating them
column16: Hand out insecticide-treated bed nets to block mosquito bites
column17: Avoid eating shellfish whenever there is a red tide
column28: Plasmodium almost always reaches a new person through the bite of an Anopheles mosquito. Treated nets block bites and kill mosquitoes, breaking the cycle. Boiling water stops Cryptosporidium, washing food helps prevent amoebic dysentery, and red tides are a dinoflagellate toxin.
column29: How does Plasmodium get from one person to the next?

column9: Why don't scientists classify Euglena as a plant or as an animal?
column14: It has no nucleus, so it doesn't fit in the plant or animal kingdom
column15: It is a single cell with both plant-like and animal-like traits
column16: It reproduces only with spores, the same way a fungus does
column17: Its cell walls are made of chitin instead of cellulose
column28: Euglena is a single eukaryotic cell with chloroplasts (plant-like) plus a flagellum, an eyespot, and the ability to take in food (animal-like). Plants and animals are multicellular, so a one-celled organism with a mix of traits fits the Kingdom Protista. It does have a nucleus, and chitin walls belong to fungi.
column29: List its plant traits and its animal traits. Then think about how many cells plants and animals have.

column9: Protista is sometimes called the "junk drawer" kingdom. Which statement best explains why?
column14: It holds eukaryotes that don't fit in the plant, animal, or fungus kingdoms
column15: It holds the organisms whose cells lack a nucleus
column16: Its members mostly break down dead material and waste
column17: Its members are too small to see without a microscope
column28: Protists are eukaryotes that are not plants, animals, or fungi, so the kingdom is a mix of very different organisms: algae, protozoans, and molds that may be one-celled or many-celled, autotrophs or heterotrophs. Organisms with no nucleus are bacteria, only some protists are decomposers, and size is not what defines the kingdom.
column29: Think about how different an amoeba, a diatom, and a slime mold are. What do they have in common?

column9: Which are ways protists help humans or ecosystems? Select all that apply.
column14: Plasmodium protects red blood cells from infection
column15: Slime molds help recycle dead organic material
column16: People eat some seaweeds, like the red alga nori
column18: Algae form the base of ocean food chains
column19: Red tides make shellfish safer to eat
column28: Algae (phytoplankton) feed ocean food chains, Euglena help keep oxygen balanced in sewage treatment, slime molds recycle organic material, and people eat red algae such as nori (the seaweed wrap on sushi). Plasmodium destroys red blood cells (malaria), and red tide toxins make shellfish dangerous to eat.
column29: Two of the choices describe harm, not help.

column9: *Entamoeba histolytica* can be swallowed as a free amoeba or as a cyst (a resting amoeba sealed inside a tough protective wall). Free amoebas usually die in the stomach, but cysts cause infection. What is the best explanation?
column14: Free amoebas move too slowly to reach the intestine
column15: Cysts can photosynthesize inside the stomach
column16: The cyst wall protects the amoeba from stomach acid
column17: Stomach acid turns free amoebas into cysts
column28: The stomach is very acidic. Free amoebas usually die there, but the tough cyst wall resists the acid. When a cyst reaches the intestine, the amoeba comes out of the cyst, divides, and causes infection. Amoebas can't photosynthesize, and acid kills amoebas rather than turning them into cysts.
column29: What harsh chemical does the stomach contain?

column9: Researchers counted *Cryptosporidium* oocysts in water: raw sewage had 5,000 oocysts per liter, and treated wastewater had 1,000 oocysts per liter. By what percent did treatment reduce the oocysts? Answer as a percent (number only).
column28: Change = 5,000 − 1,000 = 4,000 oocysts per liter. Percent reduction = 4,000 ÷ 5,000 × 100 = 80%. Treatment removed most oocysts, but 1,000 per liter still got through, so treated wastewater can still carry the parasite into lakes and rivers.
column29: Find how many were removed, then divide by the starting amount and multiply by 100.

column9: Slime molds were once classified as fungi. Which observation best supports moving them to the Kingdom Protista?
column14: They grow on rotting logs and other decaying plant material
column15: They are heterotrophs that can't make their own food
column16: They reproduce by releasing spores into the air
column17: Part of their life is a moving, amoeba-like stage that engulfs food
column28: True fungi never move, and they absorb their food. A slime mold spends part of its life as a moving, amoeba-like feeder that engulfs food, which is how animal-like protists behave. Growing on logs, being heterotrophic, and making spores are things fungi do too, so they don't separate slime molds from fungi.
column29: Which choice describes something a true fungus never does?

column9: Termites eat wood but can't digest the cellulose in it on their own. A flagellate called *Trichonympha* lives in their gut and breaks the cellulose down. What kind of relationship is this?
column14: Mutualism, because both the termite and the protist benefit
column15: Parasitism, because the protist harms the termite
column16: Commensalism, because the protist is unaffected
column17: Competition, because both want the wood
column28: The termite gets help digesting wood, and Trichonympha gets food and a home, so both benefit: mutualism. Nothing is harmed (not parasitism), and both partners are affected (not commensalism).
column29: What does each partner get out of the deal?

column9: Put the steps of how an amoeba eats in order.
column14: The food is enclosed in a food vacuole
column15: Wastes are excreted through the cell membrane
column16: Pseudopods surround a smaller organism
column17: The digested food is absorbed into the cytoplasm
column18: The food is broken down (digested) inside the vacuole
column28: An amoeba engulfs food with pseudopods (phagocytosis), the food is sealed in a food vacuole, enzymes digest it, the cytoplasm absorbs the digested food for energy, and wastes leave through the cell membrane.
column29: Food has to be captured before it can be digested, and digested before it can be absorbed.

column9: A warm-water event kills most of the single-celled floating algae in one area of the ocean. Which effect is most likely?
column14: Fish populations grow because there is less competition for sunlight
column15: Oxygen levels in the water go up
column16: Zooplankton and the fish that eat them decline because their food base is gone
column17: Water molds take over as the main producers
column28: Floating algae (phytoplankton) are the producers at the base of ocean food chains. If they die, the zooplankton that eat them decline, and so do the fish that eat zooplankton. Less photosynthesis means less oxygen, not more, and water molds are heterotrophs, so they can't be producers.
column29: Algae are at the bottom of the ocean food chain. What depends on them?

column9: Some dinoflagellates can produce their own light, making the water behind boats glow at night. This "living light" is called ___.
column28: Bioluminescence means "having living light." Some dinoflagellates (fire algae) glow, which is why sailors see a strange glow in the water behind their ships at night.
column29: It's the same thing fireflies do.

column9: Match each kind of algae to the best description.
column14: Dinoflagellates :: Fire algae that spin using two flagella
column15: Red algae :: Live deep in the ocean, where mostly blue light reaches
column16: Green algae :: Include Volvox colonies and Spirogyra
column17: Brown algae :: Large seaweeds that give food and shelter to marine animals
column28: Dinoflagellates (fire algae) usually have two flagella that make them spin. Red algae can live deep in the ocean where mostly blue light reaches. Green algae include Volvox colonies and Spirogyra. Brown algae, like kelp, are large seaweeds that feed and shelter marine animals.
column29: Use the name clues first: a "flagellate" has flagella, and kelp is the best-known big seaweed.

column9: Leo claims, "All protists are microscopic, so you can't see any of them without a microscope." Which evidence best disproves his claim?
column14: A bread mold colony can cover a whole slice of bread
column15: Giant kelp, a brown alga, can grow many meters long
column16: A shelf mushroom can grow as wide as a dinner plate
column17: A colony of bacteria on a petri dish shows up as a dot
column28: Kelp is a brown alga, a many-celled protist that forms underwater forests easily seen without a microscope. That one example disproves "all." Bread mold and shelf mushrooms are fungi, and bacteria are prokaryotes, so even though you can see them, they say nothing about protists.
column29: Which of these organisms is actually a protist?
